Topic 2 — Research (Exploratory) Data Analysis¶

3-hour seminar¶

Suggested pacing (3h):

  • 0:00–0:15 — Read through readings/objectives
  • 0:15–1:15 — Part 1: EDA techniques on a dummy dataset with injected issues
  • 1:15–1:25 — Break
  • 1:25–2:45 — Part 2: full EDA on a real Kaggle dataset (California Housing)
  • 2:45–3:00 — Wrap-up questions

Before this seminar: study the lecture material independently — this is a "no lecture" course, so treat the readings below as mandatory prep, not optional.

Learning objectives¶

  • Describe a dataset's shape, types, and quality issues systematically
  • Detect and reason about missing values and outliers
  • Use summary statistics, histograms, boxplots, and correlation heatmaps to find patterns
  • Formulate hypotheses from an EDA that a later model could test

Required readings¶

  • McKinney, Python for Data Analysis — Ch. 5, 7, 8 (Pandas basics, data cleaning, wrangling)
  • Kaggle micro-course "Pandas": https://www.kaggle.com/learn/pandas
  • Kaggle micro-course "Data Cleaning": https://www.kaggle.com/learn/data-cleaning
  • my DA course Notebooks 1 and 2

import numpy as np

Part 1 — EDA on a dummy dataset with injected problems¶

We'll build a synthetic "employee" dataset and deliberately inject missing values and outliers, so you can practice spotting them.

In [2]:
n = 300
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": np.random.normal(35, 8, n).round().astype(float),
    "salary": np.random.normal(45000, 12000, n).round(2),
    "years_exp": np.random.normal(8, 4, n).clip(0).round(1),
    "department": np.random.choice(["Sales", "Engineering", "Marketing", "HR"], n, p=[0.3, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1]),
})

# inject problems
df.loc[np.random.choice(n, 20, replace=False), "salary"] = np.nan
df.loc[np.random.choice(n, 10, replace=False), "age"] = np.nan
df.loc[np.random.choice(n, 5, replace=False), "salary"] = df["salary"].max() * 4  # outliers
df.head()

Exercise 1.2 — Distributions¶

  1. Plot a histogram of salary
  2. Plot a boxplot of salary by department
  3. Do you see anything suspicious? Explain in a markdown cell.
In [4]:
# 1. histogram of salary
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))

sns.histplot(df["salary"].dropna(), bins=30, kde=True, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Distribution of salary")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Salary")

# 2. boxplot of salary by department
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="department", y="salary", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Salary by department")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Department")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations.

  • The salary histogram is dominated by a handful of extreme values on the far right: a few points sit around 4× the maximum normal salary (~200k+ while the bulk of the distribution is between 20k and 70k). The KDE curve is almost flat because of them, and the "real" distribution is squashed into the left edge of the plot.
  • The boxplot makes the problem obvious: every department has a normal-looking box around 45k, plus a long tail of outliers above the upper whisker — and in each department a single point sits at roughly 200k. These come from the injected salary.max() * 4 values, not from any real department-level effect.
  • The department medians are almost identical, which is expected: salary was generated independently of department in the synthetic data.

Exercise 1.3 — Outlier detection with IQR¶

Write a function flag_outliers_iqr(series) that returns a boolean mask of values outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR]. Apply it to salary and count the outliers found.

In [5]:
def flag_outliers_iqr(series):
    """Boolean mask of values outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR]."""
    q1, q3 = series.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    return (series < lower) | (series > upper)


outlier_mask = flag_outliers_iqr(df["salary"])
print("Outliers found (missing salaries excluded):", outlier_mask.sum())
print()
print("Bounds for salary:",
      round(df["salary"].quantile(0.25) - 1.5 * (df["salary"].quantile(0.75) - df["salary"].quantile(0.25)), 2),
      "…",
      round(df["salary"].quantile(0.75) + 1.5 * (df["salary"].quantile(0.75) - df["salary"].quantile(0.25)), 2))
print()
print(df.loc[outlier_mask, ["salary", "department"]].sort_values("salary"))

# same flagging, convenient for any other column:
for col in ["age", "salary", "years_exp"]:
    print(f"{col:>10}: {flag_outliers_iqr(df[col]).sum()} outliers")

Exercise 2.2 — Distributions and skew¶

  1. Plot histograms for all numeric columns (df.hist(bins=50, figsize=(12,10)))
  2. Which variables look skewed? Would a log-transform help any of them?
In [9]:
housing.hist(bins=50, figsize=(12, 10))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations on skew.

  • median_house_value is capped at 500001 — a spike at the right edge. That price ceiling is a data artefact, not a real distribution; it has to be removed or handled explicitly (the rows above the cap must be dropped or clipped), otherwise the model cannot learn the true relationship for expensive districts.
  • median_income is right-skewed, but note it is already capped at ~15 (15k$/month) and expressed in tens of thousands — mostly between 1 and 6.
  • population, total_rooms, total_bedrooms, households are all strongly right-skewed with a long tail: a few districts with tens of thousands of people next to the typical few thousand. A log transform (np.log1p) would make them much closer to normal — helpful for distance-based models and for any model assuming roughly symmetric errors.
  • housing_median_age is roughly uniform with a spike at its own cap of 52 years.
  • latitude and longitude are not skewed (bimodal / geographic, no transformation needed) — they should not be log-transformed.

So: log-transform the count-like features, do not log-transform age, lat/lon or the target itself without checking the cap first.

Wrap-up questions¶

  1. List three data-quality issues you'd want to fix before modeling this dataset.
  2. Why is it good practice to do EDA on the training set only (not the full dataset)?
  3. Propose one new feature you could engineer from existing columns (e.g. rooms per household) and explain why it might help a later model.

Wrap-up answers¶

1. Three data-quality issues to fix before modeling

  1. Missing total_bedrooms (207 rows). Impute — e.g. the median within the same ocean_proximity or the median total_rooms-ratio — or drop those rows; either way the imputer must be fitted on the training set only.
  2. The target cap at median_house_value == 500001 (and the median_income / housing_median_age caps). Those rows are censored data: the model learns a flat "ceiling" region that does not exist in reality. Either drop those districts or model the value as censored / clip explicitly and document the decision.
  3. Heavy right-skew and wildly different scales in total_rooms, total_bedrooms, population, households, median_income. Fix with log transforms and/or a StandardScaler — again fitted on train only. (Runner-up: ocean_proximity is a string — it needs encoding; and there is no unit-consistent "household" feature, so room counts are not comparable between districts of different size.)

2. Why EDA on the training set only?

EDA is itself a modelling step: every decision it drives (which outliers to clip, which imputation strategy, which transforms, which features to keep, which correlations to trust) is a parameter learned from the data. If you inspect the full dataset — including the test set — then your choices are informed by the test data. That is data leakage: the test set no longer simulates truly unseen data, the reported score becomes optimistically biased, and the "hold-out" estimate can no longer be trusted. Practical recipe: split first, run all statistics and plots on train, only transform test with the fit-from-train statistics.

3. A feature to engineer: rooms per household

housing["rooms_per_household"] = housing["total_rooms"] / housing["households"]

Why it might help: raw total_rooms measures the size of the district, not the size of a home — a big district trivially has many rooms, which drowns out the information about living space. Dividing by households normalises it into "rooms per dwelling", which is close to the thing that actually determines the price per house. It usually correlates with the target more strongly than total_rooms and removes much of the population-size confound.

Once that is fixed, continue with the standard ratio features:

housing["bedrooms_ratio"] = housing["total_bedrooms"] / housing["total_rooms"]
housing["population_per_household"] = housing["population"] / housing["households"]

Houses with a low bedroom ratio are typically larger/more luxurious per room, and population_per_household captures crowding — both are known to improve California-housing models.
